references.text: Isaiah exhorts us to fear the Lord: 'The Lord, the God of hosts, him you shall hold holy. Him you shall fear, him you shall dread' (Isaiah 8:13). Jesus points in Luke 12:5 that it is God alone who deserves our fear.

The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says: 'Fear rather him who can destroy both soul and body in hell' (Matthew 10:28). This is the closest parallel to Luke 12:5, with the same message about whom we should fear.

James writes that 'one is the lawgiver and judge, he who has power to save and to destroy' (James 4:12). This emphasizes that God alone has the power to deliver the final judgment, just as Jesus stresses in Luke 12:5.

'It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God' (Hebrews 10:31). The letter to the Hebrews underscores the seriousness of standing before God's judgment, the same seriousness Jesus refers to when he exhorts his disciples to fear God.

God says: 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal' (Deuteronomy 32:39). This shows that God has power over both life and death—the very power Jesus points to when he says that God has authority to cast into Gehenna.

In the Revelation of John, the final judgment is described: 'Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. ... And if anyone was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire' (Revelation 20:14-15). This illustrates the eternal judgment that Jesus warns about in Luke 12:5.

Isaiah describes the final punishment: 'Their worm shall not die, and the fire shall not be quenched' (Isaiah 66:24). The image of Gehenna that Jesus uses in Luke 12:5 has its background partly in this text from Isaiah.
Jesus already warns in the Sermon on the Mount about the danger of 'hell fire' (Gehenna) (Matthew 5:22). This shows that Gehenna as a picture of judgment is consistent throughout Jesus' teaching.

Jesus says at the final judgment: 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels' (Matthew 25:41). This expands on the judgment Jesus points to in Luke 12:5, where the one with authority casts the ungodly into Gehenna.
'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge' (Proverbs 1:7). The fear of God that Jesus calls for in Luke 12:5 is a fundamental theme throughout wisdom literature.
